title: Why do the poles get less sun?
hook: The North Pole gets less sunlight in a year than the equator. What causes the gap?

doesNotKnow: that it is the angle of the sunlight, not extra distance from the Sun, that cuts their yearly sunlight to about two fifths of the equator's

misconception: The poles are cold because they are farther from the Sun.
objective: The learner can say that the North Pole gets about 41% of the equator's yearly top-of-atmosphere sunlight, and that the cause is the angle (the same beam spread over more ground), not its at most 6,371 km of extra distance.

claims.text: Over a year the North Pole gets about 41% of the equator's sunlight per square metre at the top of the atmosphere (51.5 N 67%, 60 N 57%, 30 N 88%).
claims.source: Daily-mean insolation Q = (S0/pi)(h0 sin(lat) sin(dec) + cos(lat) cos(dec) sin(h0)) (Berger 1978) averaged over a circular orbit in 3,600 steps: 415.5, 365.2, 277.0, 236.3 and 172.3 W/m^2 at 0, 30, 51.5, 60 and 90 N (pole/equator 0.415). Section `insol-annual` of company/domains/briefs/checks/geography-wave-j.mjs; re-run by the builder (scratchpad insol.mjs) and computed in Demo.tsx. Hartmann 2016 (Global Physical Climatology, ch. 2) shows about 417 and 173 W/m^2 (not opened by the builder).
claims.note: Derivation re-run from Demo.tsx annual(): 415.5, 365.2, 277.0, 236.3 and 172.3 W/m2, giving 100%, 88%, 67%, 57% and 41%; pole/equator 0.415. The circular-orbit average is stated in the code comment. Hartmann not opened; verified on derivation. artifacts/fact-check-wave-j/wj-econ-phys-math-geo/geo/insol.mjs.

claims.text: The pole is at most 6,371 km farther from the Sun, 0.004% of the way.
claims.source: Earth mean radius 6,371.0088 km (IUGG; EARTH_RADIUS_KM in src/kit/geo); 1 AU = 149,597,870.7 km (IAU 2012 resolution B2). At equinox the pole is R (1 - cos 90) = R farther along the Sun line than the sub-solar point: 6,371 / 149,597,870.7 = 0.0043%. Readout shown to 3 decimals: 0.004%. Sources not opened by the builder.
claims.note: Opened: WGS 84 via pyproj (a = 6,378,137 m, b = 6,356,752.314 m) gives the IUGG mean radius (2a + b)/3 = 6,371.0088 km = EARTH_RADIUS_KM in src/kit/geo; astropy gives the au as exactly 149,597,870,700 m (IAU 2012 B2). 6,371/149,597,870.7 = 0.0043%, shown 0.004%. Geometry: at equinox the pole is R farther along the Sun line than the sub-solar point (at solstice the summer pole is nearer than the centre), so 'at most'.

claims.text: That extra distance is worth less than 0.01% of the light.
claims.source: Flux falls as 1/r^2: 1 - (1 AU / (1 AU + 6,371 km))^2 = 0.0085% (section `insol-annual`).

claims.text: Near the poles the same beam lands on more ground, so each square metre gets less: at equinox noon the lit ground is 1/cos(latitude) times the beam's width (x1.61 at 51.5 N, x2.00 at 60 N), and at the pole the beam grazes the ground.
claims.source: Geometry of a parallel beam meeting a sphere at angle (90 - latitude) at equinox noon. Section `insol-annual` prints 1.00, 1.15, 1.61, 2.00. Drawn in Demo.tsx as the lit arc under a fixed-width band.
claims.note: Derivation: a parallel beam meets the ground at incidence angle = latitude at equinox noon, so it spreads over 1/cos(lat): 1.15, 1.61 and 2.00 at 30, 51.5 and 60 N, and grazes the ground at 90. Code: spread = 1/cos(lat), and at the pole the lit arc draws only the part of the band below the pole.

claims.source: Scope statement on the stage: the picture is equinox noon; the yearly share is above the air. The card makes no claim about climate zones (that needs temperature data).

claims.text: The pole still gets about 41%, not nothing: Earth's tilt gives it months of low, all-day summer sun (stage line at the pole: 'Summer tilt: months of all-day sun, never above 23°').
claims.source: Same model as c1 (Berger 1978 daily-mean insolation, circular orbit, 3,600 steps, obliquity 23.44°). Builder node re-run 2026-10-14: with obliquity 23.44° the pole has the Sun above the horizon for half the year (declination > 0), at an elevation equal to the declination, at most 23.44°; its yearly mean is 172.3 W/m^2 against the equator's 415.5 (0.415). With obliquity 0 the pole's yearly mean is 0.0 W/m^2 (share 0%), so the 41% comes from the tilt's polar summer. Solstice daily mean at the pole 541 W/m^2 vs 397 at the equator.
claims.note: Added by demo-builder (W-825, 2026-10-14); needs the fact-checker. | FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Independent numpy integration (200,000 steps, circular orbit, obliquity 23.44°, S0 1361): pole yearly mean 172.33 W/m^2 = S0 sin(eps)/pi exactly; equator 415.54; share 0.415 (41%). Sun above the horizon at the pole for half the year at elevation = declination, max 23.44° ('never above 23°'). With obliquity 0 the pole gets 0. Demo.tsx annual()/dailyQ() is the same daily-mean formula; stage line 'Summer tilt: months of all-day sun, never above 23°' holds.

recall.question: Why does a square metre near the pole get less sunlight in a year than one at the equator?
options: The same beam is spread over more ground
The pole is farther from the Sun
recall.why: Low sunlight spreads one beam over more ground. The pole's extra distance changes the light by under 0.01%.
